A system cannot accelerate itself: only an **external** force can change its momentum.
**Step 1 — identify the system.** Take the student - hair, hands and all - as one
system ✓
**Step 2 — classify the pull.** The hand pulls the hair **upward**, and by Newton's
third law the hair pulls the hand **downward** with an equal force ✓ Both forces act
**within** the system.
**Step 3 — add them up.** Internal forces always occur in equal and opposite pairs, so
they **cancel** in the total ✓ The net internal force on the system is **zero**,
however hard he pulls.
**Step 4 — apply Newton's second law.** The only external forces are **gravity** and
the **normal reaction** from the ground:
F_net = mg − N ✓
Tugging the hair changes neither, so the centre of mass cannot accelerate upward.
**Why no amount of strength would help.** The failure is not one of magnitude but of
**kind** ✓ Doubling the force doubles both members of the action-reaction pair, and
they still cancel. The first option, "the force exerted is small", misses the point
entirely.
**What the student could do instead.** Push **down on the ground** ✓ Then the ground
pushes **up** on him - an **external** force - and he rises. This is how walking,
jumping and running all work: the external agent is always the floor.
**The same principle elsewhere.**
a car accelerates through **friction from the road**, not through its engine ✓
a rocket accelerates by **ejecting mass**, so the exhaust leaves the system
no one can lift themselves by their own bootstraps - the phrase is a statement of this
law ✓
**The momentum statement.** For a system with no external force,
Σ F_ext = 0 ⟹ **p̄ constant** ✓
The centre of mass moves at constant velocity no matter what internal rearrangement
takes place.
**Reading the distractors.** "**Frictional force while gripping is small**" ✗ - even a
perfect grip would not help. "**Newton's law is not applicable to living beings**" ✗ -
the laws apply to everything ✓
∴ as the force applied is internal to the system.

Use f = (1/2L)√(T/µ) twice and take the ratio.
**Step 1 — write the original frequency.**
f₁ = (1/2L)√(T₁/µ) = **200 Hz** ✓
**Step 2 — write the new one.** The length is **doubled** to 2L and the tension is
changed to T₂:
f₂ = (1/4L)√(T₂/µ) = **300 Hz** ✓
**Step 3 — divide.**
f₂/f₁ = (1/4L)/(1/2L) x √(T₂/T₁)
300/200 = (1/2)√(T₂/T₁)
**Step 4 — solve.**
1·5 = 0·5√(T₂/T₁)
√(T₂/T₁) = 3
**T₂/T₁ = 9 : 1** ✓
**Why the tension must rise so much.** Doubling the length alone would **halve** the
frequency, from 200 Hz to 100 Hz ✓ To reach 300 Hz the tension must then raise it by a
factor of **three** - and since f ∝ √T, that needs **nine** times the tension.
**Breaking it into two steps.**
length doubled: 200 → **100 Hz**
tension multiplied by 9: 100 x √9 = 100 x 3 = **300 Hz** ✓
**Why the square root matters.** Tension enters under a root, so large changes in T give
modest changes in pitch ✓ This is why tuning a guitar string is delicate work - and why
strings must be strong enough to survive the tension a high note demands.
**A practical caution.** Nine times the tension is an enormous increase; a real string
would be near breaking ✓ The question is an exercise in the formula rather than a
description of a practicable experiment.
**The full dependence.** f = (1/2L)√(T/µ), so the frequency
rises with **√T**
falls with **1/L**
falls with **1/√µ**, for a heavier string ✓
All three are exploited in a piano: short, thin, tight strings for the treble; long,
thick, heavy ones for the bass.
**Reading the distractors.** **3 : 1** ✗ forgets that f goes as √T, not T. **1 : 9** ✗
and **1 : 3** ✗ have the tension **falling**, which would lower the pitch further after
the length has already lowered it ✓
∴ 9 : 1.

Consider the two cases separately - frictionless, and with friction.
**Step 1 — the frictionless case.** With no friction between paper and ball, the paper
slides out from under the ball and exerts **no horizontal force** on it ✓ By Newton's
first law the ball **remains stationary** relative to the table. Statement (a) is
**true**.
**Step 2 — the case with friction.** The paper, moving right, drags the ball's **bottom**
surface to the right ✓ That frictional force acts at the point of contact and produces
**two** effects:
a small forward **translation** of the centre of mass
a **torque** about the centre, which sets the ball spinning ✓
**Step 3 — work out the sense of the spin.** A rightward force applied at the **bottom**
of the ball turns it **anticlockwise** as drawn - that is, the ball is made to roll
**backwards** ✓ Once the paper is gone, friction with the table converts that spin into
backward rolling, and the ball moves to the **left**. Statement (b) is **true**.
**Step 4 — test statement (c).** It claims the ball moves **forward**, in the direction
of the pull ✓ The brief forward impulse is far smaller than the backward rolling that
the spin produces, so the ball ends up to the **left** of where it started. Statement
(c) is **false**.
**Step 5 — conclude.** **Both (a) and (b)** are correct ✓
**Why "quickly" matters.** A rapid pull gives only a brief impulse, so the forward
translation of the centre is small, while the **spin** imparted is what dominates
afterwards ✓ A slow pull would simply carry the ball along with the paper.
**The everyday demonstration.** This is the tablecloth trick in reverse ✓ Whip the cloth
out quickly and the crockery barely moves; but a **round** object, able to spin, rolls
backwards afterwards - a surprise worth trying with a marble and a strip of paper.
**The angular-momentum view.** The frictional impulse acts at a distance R below the
centre, so it delivers angular momentum about the centre as well as linear momentum ✓
Once the ball is spinning with backward sense, friction with the table does the rest.
**Reading the distractors.** "**Only a)**" ✗ and "**only b)**" ✗ each discard a true
statement. "**Only c)**" ✗ asserts the one false statement ✓
∴ both a) and b).

Extension under a given load goes as **L/r²**, so compute that ratio for each wire.
**Step 1 — write Hooke's law in terms of Young's modulus.**
Y = (F/A)/(ΔL/L)
so
ΔL = FL/(AY) = **FL/(πr²Y)** ✓
With F and Y the same for all four, **ΔL ∝ L/r²**.
**Step 2 — evaluate L/r² for each wire,** with L in cm and r in mm.
**(1)** 100/(0·2)² = 100/0·04 = **2500**
**(2)** 200/(0·4)² = 200/0·16 = **1250**
**(3)** 300/(0·6)² = 300/0·36 = **833**
**(4)** 400/(0·8)² = 400/0·64 = **625** ✓
**Step 3 — pick the largest.** The **first** wire, with L = 100 cm and r = 0·2 mm, has
much the greatest value and therefore the **largest extension** ✓
**Why the thinnest wire wins despite being the shortest.** The radius enters as a
**square** while the length enters only linearly ✓ Going from wire 1 to wire 4, the
length grows fourfold but the radius also grows fourfold, so r² grows **sixteenfold** -
and 4/16 = 1/4, leaving wire 4 with a quarter of wire 1's extension.
**The pattern in the numbers.** Each wire has both L and r multiplied by the same
factor, so L/r² falls as **1/n**:
2500, 1250, 833, 625 ✓ exactly 2500 divided by 1, 2, 3 and 4.
**The stress view.** Stress is F/A, and the thinnest wire has the smallest area, so it
carries the **greatest stress** ✓ The same strain-per-unit-stress applies to all, so the
most stressed wire stretches most per unit length - and being short does not save it.
**The practical consequence.** A thin wire breaks first under a shared load ✓ which is
why load-bearing cables are specified by **cross-section**, not by length.
**Consistency of units.** Mixing cm for length and mm for radius is harmless here,
because only the **ratios** are compared ✓ All four are treated the same way.
∴ L = 100 cm, r = 0.2 mm.

A transformer works by **mutual induction** between two coils linked by a common
magnetic flux.
**Step 1 — describe the mechanism.** Alternating current in the **primary** sets up a
changing magnetic flux in the iron core ✓ That flux threads the **secondary**, and by
Faraday's law the changing flux induces an emf in it:
e_s = −N_s dΦ/dt ✓
**Step 2 — name the effect.** An emf induced in **one** coil by a changing current in
**another** is **mutual induction** ✓
**Step 3 — note the quantity that measures it.** The mutual inductance M:
e_s = −M dI_p/dt ✓
It depends on the geometry of the two coils and on the core linking them.
**Why self-induction is not the answer.** Self-induction is the emf a coil induces in
**itself** ✓ It certainly occurs in the primary - the back-emf that limits the primary
current - but it is not what transfers energy to the secondary. The question asks for
the principle the **transformer** works on, and that is the coupling between two coils.
**Why the iron core matters.** It confines the flux and guides almost all of it through
the secondary, raising the coupling towards 1 ✓ The core is **laminated** to suppress
eddy currents, which would otherwise waste energy as heat.
**The turns relation that follows.** With the same flux through each turn of both
coils,
**V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p** ✓
and by conservation of energy, I_s/I_p = N_p/N_s. Both follow directly from mutual
induction.
**Why a transformer will not work on d.c.** A steady current produces a **constant**
flux, so dΦ/dt = 0 and no emf is induced ✓ Transformers are a.c. devices by their very
nature.
**Reading the distractors.** **Self induction** ✗ is the single-coil effect.
**Electrical inertia** ✗ is a loose description of **inductance** in general, not a
principle. **Magnetic effect of current** ✗ describes how the primary makes a field -
necessary but not sufficient, since without a **changing** field nothing is induced ✓
∴ mutual induction.

At the angle where sliding just begins, the limiting friction exactly balances the
component of gravity along the slope.
**Step 1 — resolve the weight on the incline.**
along the slope: **mg sin θ**
perpendicular to it: **mg cos θ** = N ✓
**Step 2 — write the condition for impending motion.** Sliding begins when the required
friction reaches its maximum value µ_s N:
mg sin θ = µ_s (mg cos θ) ✓
**Step 3 — cancel and solve.**
**µ_s = tan θ** ✓
**What this angle is called.** The **angle of repose** ✓ It is also the **angle of
friction** - the greatest angle by which the total contact force can lean from the
normal - and the two are numerically equal for this reason.
**Why the mass does not matter.** Both the driving force and the maximum friction carry
the factor **mg**, which cancels ✓ A heavy block and a light one begin to slide at
exactly the same angle, which is what makes the tilt method a practical way of
measuring µ.
**Why µ can exceed 1.** tan θ grows without limit as θ approaches 90°, so a coefficient
above 1 simply means a surface so grippy that the block holds on a slope steeper than
45° ✓ Rubber on dry tarmac reaches about 1·0 to 1·5.
**A worked value.** For µ = 0·5:
θ = tan⁻¹(0·5) = **26·6°** ✓ so the block rests on anything gentler and slides on
anything steeper.
**What happens beyond the angle.** Once sliding starts, **kinetic** friction takes over,
and µ_k is usually a little **less** than µ_s ✓ so the block accelerates with
a = g(sin θ − µ_k cos θ) rather than creeping.
**Why the other options fail on principle.** µ is a **dimensionless** number whose range
is 0 to ∞ ✓ **sin θ** and **cos θ** are both bounded by 1, so neither could describe a
surface with µ > 1; **sec θ** is never less than 1, so it could not describe a slippery
surface at all. Only **tan θ** spans the full range.
∴ tan θ.

On a level curve, friction alone supplies the centripetal force, so there is a maximum
safe speed.
**Step 1 — write the condition for not slipping.** The friction available must meet the
centripetal demand:
mv²/r ≤ µ mg ✓
**Step 2 — cancel the mass and rearrange.**
**v² ≤ µrg** ✓
**Step 3 — substitute.**
v²_max = (0·1)(5)(10)
= **5 m² s⁻²** ✓
so the greatest safe speed is v = √5 = **2·24 m s⁻¹**.
**Step 4 — compare with the actual speed.** The driver is doing **5 m s⁻¹**, so
v² = **25**, far above the limit of 5 ✓ The vehicle **will** slip.
**Step 5 — state the condition as the options do.** Slipping occurs whenever
**v² > 5 m² s⁻¹** ✓ which is the second option.
**Why the mass drops out.** A heavier vehicle needs more centripetal force but also
presses harder on the road and so generates proportionally more friction ✓ The limiting
speed is the same for a loaded lorry and a small car on the same surface.
**How fast the driver could safely go.** Only **2·24 m s⁻¹**, about 8 km/h ✓ A sharp
5 m bend on a slippery road (µ = 0·1) must be taken at walking pace - which is why such
bends are banked.
**How banking helps.** On a track banked at angle θ the normal force supplies part of
the centripetal force, and the safe speed becomes
v² = rg(µ + tan θ)/(1 − µ tan θ) ✓
much larger than µrg. With θ = 30° and the same µ and r, the safe speed more than
doubles.
**A note on the printed units.** The options write "v² = 5 m s⁻¹", though v² is properly
in **m² s⁻²** ✓ The intended comparison - of v² against the number 5 - is clear.
**Reading the distractors.** "**Slips if v² = 5**" ✗ is the exact threshold, where it
only just holds. "**Slips if v² < 5**" ✗ reverses the inequality. "**Will not slip if
v² > 10**" ✗ is doubly wrong ✓
∴ a person will slip if v² > 5 ms⁻¹.

The Curie-Weiss law describes a ferromagnet **after** it has lost its ferromagnetism -
that is, **above** the Curie temperature.
**Step 1 — state the law.**
χ = C/(T − T_C) ✓
with C the Curie constant and T_C the Curie temperature.
**Step 2 — see where it can apply.** The expression requires **T > T_C**; at T = T_C the
susceptibility diverges, and below it the formula is meaningless ✓ So the law holds
**above** the Curie temperature.
**Step 3 — see what happens physically there.** Above T_C the thermal agitation destroys
the alignment of the magnetic domains, and iron ceases to be ferromagnetic ✓ It becomes
an ordinary **paramagnet**, and the Curie-Weiss law is the paramagnetic law with a
correction for the residual exchange interaction.
**Iron's Curie temperature.** **1043 K**, about 770 °C ✓ Heat an iron nail to red heat
and a magnet no longer attracts it; let it cool and the attraction returns.
**What happens below T_C.** The exchange interaction aligns neighbouring atomic moments
into **domains**, giving spontaneous magnetisation and hysteresis ✓ The susceptibility
is then enormous and depends on the field and on the sample's history, so no simple
formula like χ = C/(T − T_C) can describe it.
**The contrast with the plain Curie law.** For a **paramagnet** with no interaction
between moments,
χ = C/T ✓
The Curie-Weiss law is this with T replaced by (T − T_C) - the shift measuring the
strength of the interaction that the thermal motion must overcome.
**Why χ grows as T falls towards T_C.** The denominator shrinks, so the material becomes
ever easier to magnetise ✓ At T_C it orders spontaneously and the ferromagnetic phase
begins - a classic second-order phase transition.
**A practical use.** Some rice cookers and soldering irons use a **Curie-point switch**:
a ferromagnetic element loses its magnetism at a set temperature and releases a spring,
cutting the power ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **Below T_C** ✗ is the ferromagnetic region, where the law
fails. **At T_C only** ✗ is the single point where χ diverges. **At all temperatures** ✗
ignores the breakdown below T_C ✓
∴ above Curie temperature.
